summary: Storm Response Mission Design Lab is a browser-based game. A solar storm like the real one of May 2024 has disabled the satellites that served a region. You lead four engineer who design, test, launch and fly a small CubeSat mission within one year: an emergency messaging backup for the region. In one year you and your 3 friend rebuild the all communications systems. Everyone is responsible for creating a different part of the satellite, according to their own area of ​​expertise. Everyone has a hidden task of their own and tries to carry it out without letting others notice.
details:
What this game is

Storm Response: Mission Design Lab is a browser game made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, challenge "Space Mission Design Game". A solar storm like the real one of May 2024 has disabled the satellites that served a region. You lead four scientists who design, test, launch and fly a small CubeSat mission within one year: an emergency messaging backup for the region.

How to play

  1. Briefing. Pick the storm region and the resources you think will be tight. Listen to the four scientists: each one has a hidden goal and only drops hints.
  2. Workshop. Build the satellite from parts. Watch mass, power, budget, data, communication and time. Check feasibility before you approve.
  3. Test lab. Choose a full or a short test campaign. A short test saves time but makes a failure more likely.
  4. Launch and mission control. Watch the passes over the region. When the storm arrives, decide: keep measuring or go to safe mode.
  5. Debrief. See the score breakdown, every hidden goal revealed, and the real mission yours is most similar to. Then try another design.

How we used AI

The core concept (a solar storm, a replacement communication satellite, four scientists) came from our team. The scene draft and the Hidden Agendas mechanic were suggested by Claude (Anthropic); our team chose and adapted them. We used Claude to check the concept against the challenge and NASA sources, fix logical errors, suggest instruments and real-mission comparisons, draft the design document, and write the game code with Claude Code. Every AI-assisted source file starts with an 'AI-assisted' header comment. Visuals are made in code and with NASA imagery (Blue Marble, Black Marble, SDO), credited in Sources; no AI image generators were used.

How It Works – Key Technical Innovations

  1. Physics-Based Engineering Budgets: Every spacecraft the player builds is checked live against eight budgets, the same ones a real CubeSat team tracks:
    • Mass & Volume: frame plus part masses, compared with the CubeSat Design Specification limits (6 kg for 3U, 12 kg for 6U).
    • Power: orbit-average generation = panel area × solar constant × cell efficiency × sun factor × (1 − eclipse fraction). The eclipse comes from a cylindrical Earth shadow at a worst-case beta angle. The battery must carry the satellite through each eclipse within a safe depth of discharge.
    • Communication: contact minutes with the storm region’s gateway stations, from the visibility angle λ = acos(R·cos ε / (R + h)) − ε. A day is simulated in 20-second steps and averaged over 8 orbit start positions.
    • Data, Budget, Time, Orbit Life: daily MB produced vs. downlinked, full program cost with a 10% reserve, a month-by-month calendar to the next launch slot, and orbital period T = 2π√(a³/μ) with storm-shortened lifetime checked against the FCC 5-year disposal rule.
  2. Real Space-Weather Data: The storm is built on NASA DONKI records of the May 2024 geomagnetic storm (Kp values, flare times, CME shock arrival) and real NASA SDO/AIA Sun images from 10–11 May 2024. The storm heats and swells the upper atmosphere, so low orbits lose lifetime, as happened to the Starlink satellites lost in February 2022. A 30-day operations phase then plays out day by day. Ground-station outages hit the network, and when a second extreme storm arrives the team must choose: keep measuring and risk the hardware, or switch to safe mode and lose the storm data.
  3. NASA-Style Requirements & Verification: The mission has four requirements: launch in 12 months, communication with the storm region, daily storm data, and one year of operation. Each is verified with NASA’s four methods: Test, Analysis, Inspection and Demonstration. Players choose a full or short test campaign. The short test saves time but raises the failure chance, and the reserve budget pays for any repair. Every part in the catalogue is tied to a real mission (MinXSS, Dellingr and others) through a sources file. Values that are estimates are marked “est.” on screen.
  4. Team Roles with Hidden Goals: Four players share one device (pass-and-play). Each role owns its own decisions, such as orbit, calendar and launcher, or relay, ground stations and money. Each player also holds a hidden goal (for example “Protect the reserve”). Asking the mission-control advisor reveals one hidden goal, but it costs half a month of team time from the reserve. At the debrief all goals are revealed, and the team sees how well it balanced them.
    • Employed bees change one decision and keep it only if the score rises.
    • Onlooker bees pick sources in proportion to their score.
    • Scout bees replace a source that stops improving with a new random valid design.
    • The colony has 20 sources and runs 150 cycles in a Web Worker. It never designs for the player during the game.
  5. Explainable Debrief & Real-Mission Match: Every lost point gets a “Why?” explanation. The final design is matched to the real CubeSat mission it most resembles, with sourced facts. Each design can also be saved as a short checksummed code, so the run can be replayed exactly.
